https://www.dw.com/en/germany-arrests-uk.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5INZK The investigation was being carried out under the auspices of a new national centre to coordinate defences against "hybrid attacks" Image: Hendrik Schmidt/dpa/picture alliance Advertisement German authorities have arrested a Ukrainian man suspected of spying on a defense company in Bavaria to prepare possible acts of sabotage. Investigators suspect he took photographs of the premises of a Bavarian defense company in June and passed them to handlers working for a foreign intelligence service. What do we know about the case so far? The 33-year-old was detained in the eastern state of Thuringia on Sunday and is now in pretrial detention, Munich prosecutors and Bavaria's State Criminal Police Office said on Thursday . A Munich court issued an arrest warrant on Monday and the suspect is now being held in pre-trial detention in Bavaria. Authorities described the man as a so-called "low-level agent," a term used for people recruited by foreign intelligence services to carry out relatively simple tasks. Prosecutors said he was suspected of acting as an agent for sabotage purposes. The arrest followed cooperation between security and intelligence agencies coordinated through Germany's recently established Joint Center for Countering Hybrid Threats , known as GAZ-Hybrid. Authorities did not identify the foreign intelligence service allegedly involved and said no further details could be released while the investigation continues. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cp30.text: Figure caption, Watch: Huge blaze after attack on petrol tank in Libya By Basillioh Rukanga Published 4 hours ago Libyan emergency services have been battling to contain a huge blaze at a major oil plant after it was targeted by unknown attackers. The Zawiya refinery, west of the capital Tripoli, was hit in a drone strike on Monday evening - the third such incident in two days. The National Oil Corporation (NOC) said a tank containing about 4.5m litres of fuel was directly hit, triggering a huge fire that caused it to collapse. It said it was considering suspending operations if the attacks continued. There were no "serious injuries" from the fire, with most patients treated for smoke inhalation, Libya's Ambulance and Emergency Service said on Tuesday. The Zawiya refinery is the largest operational facility in Libya, with an output of 120,000 barrels per day. The NOC condemned similar attacks in past days in Zawiya, including two drone strikes on a naphtha reservoir and a water desalination plant. It called on the authorities to investigate who was behind the violence. The attacks have highlighted continuing instability in Libya, which has been split in two since a civil war broke out after the ousting of former leader Muammar Gaddafi. Colonel Gaddafi seized power in 1969 and ruled autocratically for four decades until he was toppled and killed in 2011 in a rebellion assisted by Western military intervention Since his fall, rival power centres, one based in the east backed by military commander Khalifa Haftar, and one in the west in Tripoli, led by Prime Minister Abdulhamid Dbeibah, have been jostling for political and military dominance. Photograph: AP S (uk)/Alamy View image in fullscreen Manchester airport. Most of the accessed data related to wifi sign-ups in the three airports’ terminals. Photograph: AP S (uk)/Alamy Airline industry Three UK airports hit by cyber-attack with data of 8.7m customers accessed Company that runs Manchester, Stansted and East Midlands hubs says passenger safety is unaffected Business live – latest updates Lauren Almeida Thu 27 Aug 2026 10.53 EDT First published on Thu 27 Aug 2026 08.21 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Manchester, London Stansted and East Midlands airports have been hit by a cyber-attack in which hackers accessed the data of about 8.7 million customers. The incident involved data related to “car park, lounge and fast-track bookings and in-airport wifi sign-ups”, and the hackers obtained email addresses, phone numbers, vehicle registration numbers and postcodes, said Manchester Airports Group (MAG), which operates the three hubs. The company said that “at no point has passenger safety or aviation security been compromised” during the incident and operations at the airports were unaffected. The hacked system did not hold customers’ bank or payment details. View image in fullscreen An email sent to an affected customer from London Stansted airport. Photograph: Yui Mok/PA In an email to customers, London Stansted said: “We would urge you to be particularly cautious of unexpected emails, calls or text messages claiming to be from us. We will never contact you unexpectedly to ask for payment or banking information. We apologise for any inconvenience or concern this may cause.” The cyber-attack hit the airports during the peak summer travel season. Many families are flying back into the UK this week before the start of the new school year. Fifty-four million passengers flew through Manchester, London Stansted and East Midlands airports combined last year. A MAG spokesperson said the company had “immediately contained the risk” from the incident and was “working with specialist advisers and taking appropriate steps to protect our customers and systems”. “We have informed and are working with the relevant authorities. At no point has passenger safety or aviation security been compromised,” they said. “Airport operations remain unaffected and customer parking services continue to operate normally. “We would like to reassure customers that Manchester Airport Group takes the security of customer information extremely seriously and we apologise for any inconvenience or concern caused.” Lauren Wills-Dixon, a partner at the law firm Gordons, said the scale of the attack was notable. “Airports sell a number of services including lounge access, parking and fast-track bookings. Wi-fi access also requires customers to input their data,” she said. “As a result, operators will hold large amounts of customer data and this, together with the increased use of technology, only increases the threat of a cyber-attack.” The incident comes as pressure grows on suppliers and operators of national infrastructure to improve their cyber-defences. Flights were delayed and cancelled last year at three major European airports – including London’s largest, Heathrow – after the company behind the software used for check-in and boarding said it had been hit by a cyber-attack . Hackers linked to Iran were blamed earlier this month for a cyber-attack that caused the temporary shutdown of a British power plant. The government said the incident involved a small-scale generator and that at no point was there a risk to the wider energy system. There was a wave of high-profile cyber-attacks against British companies last year, ranging from one that shut down the operations of Jaguar Land Rover for weeks to others targeting Marks & Spencer , Harrods and the Co-op food chain . Soybean plants on the right were planted later in the season and stand taller, on 9 August 2017. Photograph: The Washington Post/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Soybean plants on the left show signs of being affected by Dicamba (stunted growth, curled up leaves, low bean yield.) Soybean plants on the right were planted later in the season and stand taller, on 9 August 2017. Photograph: The Washington Post/Getty Images Trump administration US environment agency let Bayer pick regulations for destructive weedkiller, documents show Environmental Protection Agency asked firm to choose rules it wanted for dicamba, then put the choices in a proposed federal rule Tom Perkins Sun 20 Sep 2026 08.00 EDT Last modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 08.01 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The EPA allowed pesticide giant Bayer to pick from a menu of regulation options for the controversial and destructive weedkiller dicamba, newly released internal agency documents show. The documents provide an unusually clear look into the process of developing pesticide regulations, which is typically done out of public view. It shows in detail how the EPA asked Bayer which regulations it wanted, received a response from Bayer, then put Bayer’s choices into a proposed federal rule. Dicamba is drift prone and kills vegetation and crops for miles around fields where it is sprayed, and is linked to liver cancer and Non-Hodgkin lymphoma. Courts have twice ordered it off the market because of its drift problems, but the EPA has re-approved it. US ends limits on coal and gas plant emissions, removing key tool to fight climate crisis Read more The EPA solicited Bayer’s input on the level of restrictions to limit dicamba volatility and runoff, ranging from more protective to less protective, records released in ongoing litigation over the substance show. The EPA concluded one presentation with a slide entitled “Registrant response needed” which posed the question “Which mitigation option to go forward with?” Bayer chose the least protective for one regulation, and the middle of three levels of protection for another regulation. It also got one other change it requested into the rule. Pesticide regulations are typically a negotiation between industry and the EPA, but the exchange that the documents reveal is “crossing a line”, said Nathan Donley, environmental health science director with the Center for Biological Diversity, which is litigating on the issue. “The EPA is allowing Bayer to choose its preferred measures to limit dicamba’s damage as if it was ordering up a late-night dinner à la carte from Chili’s,” Donley said. “It becomes troublesome when the EPA allows them to regulate themselves by choosing the mitigations.” The Center for Biological Diversity and the Center for Food Safety brought the lawsuit. The documents come as the EPA has faced criticism for stacking its leadership with industry veterans. The top four toxics office positions at the EPA are held by former chemical industry leaders, including Kyle Kunkler, a former pesticide industry lobbyist who is now a deputy assistant administrator and oversees the pesticides program. Despite repeated assurances from the EPA that it has put effective protections in place, dicamba drift has damaged millions of acres of farmland and caused damage to orchards, vegetable farms, home gardens, native plants, trees and wildlife refuges across the country since its first approval in 2016. Experts have found dicamba drift damage to be the worst of any herbicide in the history of US agriculture. Still, the current approval provides even fewer protections from dicamba drift and damage than past approvals, the lawsuit alleges. In a statement to the Guardian, an EPA spokesperson said: “Make no mistake: this is not a compliance failure; it is the regulatory system working exactly as intended.” “The agency notifies the [pesticide maker] and works with them to identify possible solutions” to risks, the spokesperson wrote. “[Companies] are permitted to submit mitigation ideas that preserve their product’s utility, and EPA also will independently develop its own proposed mitigations. To be explicitly clear: the registrant does not dictate terms.” During a May 2025 EPA meeting with Bayer, the agency gave Bayer two mitigation choices that would allegedly address dicamba’s high volatility, which is what makes it drift prone. A more restrictive option would have prevented dicamba applications above 85F, and a less restrictive option would allow applications up to 95F, if the acreage treated was reduced. California bans paraquat, highly toxic herbicide outlawed in more than 70 countries Read more The EPA also gave Bayer three options for addressing dicamba runoff, documents show. It then concluded the presentation with a solicitation for Bayer to decide. An EPA manager then wrote in an email that “the next step in the process beyond the [presentation] is getting feedback from the registrants on what mitigation and mitigation implementation option they would like to move forward with”. Separate documents obtained by the Center for Biological Diversity showed the plan was presented to Nancy Beck, a controversial former lobbyist for the American Chemistry Council who now leads the EPA’s office of chemical safety. The revelations drew condemnation from “make America healthy again” (Maha) advocate Kelly Ryerson, who said: “It is now undeniable that the EPA remains fully captured by a crooked collection of pesticide company players who so enthusiastically ignore the substantial losses of farmers and the federal courts who mandated a halt to dicamba use.” Eight days later, a representative from Bayer emailed the EPA: “After discussion with EPA and reviewing these options carefully, Bayer would like to proceed as described below … ” Bayer chose the less restrictive option for volatility mitigation, which would allow it to be applied at up to 95 degrees as long as the dicamba-treated area would be reduced. Bayer also wanted another option that the EPA had not proposed, emails show. It would allow full-field dicamba treatments at higher temperatures if dicamba was not tank mixed. The EPA granted both requests, and Bayer’s preferred option for mitigating run off. These were included in the rules proposed a few months later, documents show. “In return for this egregiousness, I would like the EPA to propose a menu of options to Maha for significantly decreasing our exposure to known carcinogens and endocrine disruptors,” Ryerson added. At the same time, he denied plans to attack neighboring countries, saying such a move would be “tantamount to death” because Belarus could not win a conflict against the powerful states surrounding it. by Kyiv Post | Sept. 11, 2026, 4:56 pm Flip Share Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Bluesky Email Copy Copied In this pool photograph distributed by the Russian state agency Sputnik, Belarus' President Alexander Lukashenko attends a SCO+ format meeting of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) summit in Bishkek on September 1, 2026. (Photo by Vyacheslav PROKOFYEV / POOL / AFP) Content Share Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Bluesky Email Copy Copied Flip Belarusian leader Alexander Lukashenko said the country could test its armed forces “up to and including mobilization,” while insisting that attacking neighboring states would be “tantamount to death” for Belarus on Friday, Sept. 11. According to Belarusian state news agency BelTA , Lukashenko made the remarks during a visit to the Obuz-Lesnovsky combined-arms training ground near Baranavichy. JOIN US ON TELEGRAM Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official . “I already said it in plain language: the army needs to be shaken up. The time has come. The whole army. We will check everyone,” Lukashenko said. His statement did not amount to an announcement of an immediate nationwide mobilization. He provided no details about how many reservists could be called up or when such an exercise might take place. Advertisement Lukashenko said an artillery brigade was currently undergoing an inspection at his order, following earlier checks of tank and motorized rifle units. “We are doing everything as it would be in war,” he said, adding that the exercises incorporated lessons from modern military conflicts. “We could not win such a conflict” In separate remarks during the military visit, Lukashenko claimed Belarus had no plans to attack its neighbors. “We are pragmatists. We understand that if we attacked someone, one of our neighbors, for example, it would be tantamount to death,” he said, according to remarks published by the Pul Pervogo Telegram channel and reported by RBC-Ukraine . “We could not win a conflict against the ‘monsters’ located around our perimeter. Why start a war then?” he added. Other Topics of Interest Same Appeasement, Same Mistakes Kushner and Witkoff visited Moscow and Kyiv. Rather than making any progress toward peace, they exposed a weak spot in US foreign policy. Lukashenko said Belarus would never attack first but insisted that its authorities had an obligation to protect “every millimeter” of the country’s territory, even if doing so cost lives. The Belarusian leader also asked Defense Minister Viktor Khrenin whether the military command system could be deployed if war broke out. “What if there is a war?” Lukashenko asked. “We are ready to deploy,” Khrenin replied. The defense minister said the system could manage the armed forces, government agencies, and the civilian sector during a conflict. Advertisement “What we have now, we could only dream about five years ago,” Khrenin said. Belarus and Russia’s war Despite Lukashenko’s assurances, Belarus remains Russia’s closest regional ally and has played a significant supporting role in Moscow’s war against Ukraine. Minsk allowed Russia to use Belarusian territory and military infrastructure to launch its full-scale invasion in February 2022. Russian troops, aircraft, and weapons have continued operating from the country, although Belarus has not formally deployed its forces to fight in Ukraine. Belarus also borders three NATO members – Poland, Lithuania, and Latvia – and frequently conducts joint military exercises with Russia, fueling security concerns along the alliance’s eastern flank. https://www.straitstimes.com/world/europ.text: Italian NATO jet downs suspected Russian drone over Lithuania Sign up now: Get ST's newsletters delivered to your inbox Published Sep 15, 2026, 06:31 AM Updated Sep 16, 2026, 01:31 AM Set as preferred source Listen SIAULIAI AIR BASE, Lithuania, Sept 15 - An Italian fighter jet deployed on a NATO mission shot down a drone in Lithuanian airspace on Tuesday that "most probably" came from Russia, Italian Defence Minister Guido Crosetto said. Lithuanian authorities said on Tuesday they are still investigating the origin of the debris. A Ukrainian military source told Reuters the debris in the images appeared to be from a Geran-2, a long-range attack drone widely used by Russia. Russia did not immediately comment on the incident. If confirmed, it would be the first known instance of a Russian military drone entering Lithuania, a NATO and European Union member, since the summer of 2025, when two Russian drones accidentally crashed in the country. The drone entered Lithuanian airspace from Belarus, a Russian ally, after midnight and was shot down near the southern village of Pratkunai not far from the city of Kaunas, the Lithuanian national crisis management centre said. "Last night, again, the Italian pilots have intervened and they have shot down a threat that most probably came from Russia", Crosetto told reporters at Siauliai Air Base, where Italian fighters are based as part of the NATO Baltic Air Defence mission. "The presence of Italian aircraft here is the clear demonstration of the value of the Atlantic alliance for Italy and what it means to be an ally", he said after meeting crews with Lithuanian Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas. Kaunas said on social media the drone carried an explosive. The Lithuanian Army shared video from the site of the crash, showing debris scattered in the grass. Some of the parts appeared to be made of wood and some appeared charred. A drone alert had been issued in the Lithuanian capital Vilnius and Kaunas and the surrounding regions after the drone was detected. DRONE ALERT Ukrainian drones have repeatedly entered NATO airspace in the Baltic region in recent months. Kyiv says they were steered off course by Russian signal jamming. This has stoked concerns that Russia's war in Ukraine is spilling over NATO's borders. Fighters with the NATO Baltic Air Defence mission have patrolled the skies of Latvia, Lithuania and Estonia since the Baltic countries joined the alliance in 2004. The mission's jets shot down stray Ukrainian drones over Estonia in May, and over Latvia in June and August. Ukraine has stepped up long-range drone attacks on Russia, including in the Baltic Sea area. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cv98.text: Figure caption, Two of the victims were five-year-old Rhoam Summer (left) and teacher Meghan Lambert, 25 (right) By Sareen Habeshian and Nardine Saad Published 17 October 2026, 00:02 BST Updated 1 hour ago Some readers may find this article distressing. An Oregon teacher threw her mobile phone before she tackled and tried to wrestle away a shotgun from the arms of a teen suspect who opened fire on a special educational needs class. As she tussled with him on the floor of the class - where three children and a teacher were killed - a bystander armed with a pistol ran inside and killed the teen. The bystander, a father of two girls at the school, had been driving past Silver Rail Elementary in Bend on Thursday lunchtime when he saw the suspect firing in the car park, then shooting through a window to enter. Police said the 16-year-old suspect used to be a student at the school. Police say the suspect was armed with about 44 more rounds of shotgun ammunition when he was stopped. He fired as many as 15 rounds in the class. "To the people who showed courage in the face of such violence, and intervened to prevent this tragedy from being any worse, we owe you a debt of gratitude," Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz said on Friday. Police offered more information on the attack at a news conference on Friday, where they identified two of the four victims. They include five-year-old Rhoam Summer and 25-year-old teacher Meghan Lambert. The families of the two other students who were killed, an eight-year-old and 11-year-old, did not wish to have them publicly identified yet, police said. Two others were injured in the attack. Another teacher, a 54-year-old, was still being treated at hospital, and a seven-year-old student, who was in serious but stable condition. Figure caption, Watch: Mother of Oregon school shooting 'hero' recounts call with son Krantz said the heroic actions of both the teacher and the father who ran inside the school saved lives. He said the teacher who wrestled with the gunman was not hurt but "almost certainly helped prevent more bloodshed". He identified the suspect as 16-year-old Griffin J John II, who previously attended the school and was a special educational needs student there. A search warrant has been executed at the suspect's home and a search is ongoing, the police chief said. Police believe the suspect travelled to the elementary school on foot, but they are still investigating his exact movements and how he acquired the gun. A motive is also not clear. Officials did not confirm the name of the father who intervened and fatally shot the suspect. But Kaylub Giamanco's family has identified him to US media as the person who sprang into action. The 36-year-old carpenter had just finished lunch and was on his way home when he passed the school, his brother told NBC News. He saw the suspect open fire on a vehicle outside the school then shoot through a window and go inside. Image source, Getty Images Police said he had a legally concealed .40 calibre in his vehicle and his brother said he grabbed the pistol "and decided to go in after" the suspect. Police say he fired at the suspect "multiple times", killing him. Giamanco's mother, Kenda Freeman, who lives in Sacramento, California, told a local CBS station her son had called her moments after the shooting, and he was "traumatised". "He said a man went into my daughter's school," Freeman said, pausing as she started to tear up. "And, um, shot kids. And he said, and I looked at him point blank, and I shot and killed him, mom." She added: "I told him he saved a lot of lives, and he said, mom, I couldn't save them all." US President Donald Trump praised the bystander on Friday, calling him a "great hero". Addressing reporters at the White House before departing for Georgia, Trump said the situation could have been "much worse" with no intervention. "It's a terrible thing, but thank goodness for a man that had a gun and knew how to use it," he said. Without naming the bystander, Oregon Governor Tina Kotek acknowledged the man's heroic actions stopping further loss of life, but noted they "carry a heavy emotional burden, and I just want you to know that my thoughts are with you as well". Kayla Epstein contributed to this report.
